item.content:encoded:
The VMware portfolio is evolving to support telcos in operating the infrastructure that runs some of the most demanding, mission-critical workloads. At Broadcom, our commitment to telcos remains, and we are now better positioned to apply the scale and breadth of our enterprise expertise to the telecommunications industry while meeting carrier-grade requirements.

The telecommunications industry continues to face mounting pressure to modernize networks and lower costs. Hardware costs are rising sharply, and global demand for memory driven by AI continues to create supply chain challenges, pushing server costs even higher. Agentic AI adds to the pressure, as operators need infrastructure to monetize AI workloads in addition to their network functions. The move to containerized, cloud-native architectures has created new operational silos, each with its own stack to manage.

Running these on separate platforms means investing in and managing separate infrastructure stacks at the moment hardware is most expensive. Telcos need a single platform that runs network functions, cloud-native workloads, and AI with carrier-grade reliability, so they can get more from the hardware they already own and scale as demand grows. 

The next step is consolidating telco-grade capabilities and advanced enterprise features into a unified platform for telcos.

A Modernized Platform for Telcos

VMware software has served telcos from the start of network functions virtualization (NFV), helping the telecommunications industry transform and paving the way for the migration to software. We built a vast ecosystem of virtual network functions (VNFs) with choice at its heart, provided telco customers with a carrier-grade NFV platform, and supported them with openness and choice where they matter most. 

Our investment in the telecommunications industry continues to deepen. Telcos operate some of the most demanding, mission-critical workloads in the world, and the infrastructure that underpins telco workloads must be engineered to telco-grade standards from the ground up. 

We have been rethinking how to best support telcos. We want telcos to get the maximum value from the engineering effort that goes into supporting our more than hundreds of thousands of enterprise customers. Rather than continuing to develop Telco Cloud Platform as a standalone platform, we are now fully supporting telcos through VMware Cloud Foundation Telco (VCF Telco), which builds on the core capabilities of the cross-industry VMware Cloud Foundation.

As part of this, the standalone VMware Telco Cloud Platform licensing SKUs reach End of Availability (EOA) on November 2, 2026 and are fulfilled through the VCF license and SKU going forward. Customers purchasing the VCF SKU continue to receive existing Telco features as well as upcoming new features and enhancements under development for the telco segment. Many operators already run VCF for IT. Delivering telco on the same VCF platform lets them run virtual and cloud-native network functions, IT workloads, and AI on one stack with one operating model, rather than maintaining separate network and IT clouds.

Built Telco-Grade, Telco-Ready

VCF is engineered to telco-grade standards through its design, testing, security hardening, and performance tuning, so it is telco-ready out of the box. VCF Telco takes the strong capabilities of VCF that are trusted by enterprises and equips the platform with the features telcos need to deliver performant, secure, agile, and energy-efficient networks. Telcos are core to VCF, and they receive continued investment and extension with every release. We continue to expand our telco partner validations aligned with standard telco architectures. 

The capabilities built into VCF Telco include:

  • Carrier-grade reliability and resiliency engineered for always-on infrastructure, with high availability, fault tolerance, backup and restore, and disaster recovery, built on software-defined networking and software-defined storage to meet the stringent uptime requirements of telecom networks.
  • Fleet management delivers operational simplicity with one management domain for IT and telco workloads from data center to edge, zero-touch lifecycle management that requires no onsite IT, and shared observability through VCF Operations and VCF Operations for logs.
  • AI-native infrastructure with VMware Private AI Services built in, with support for fully air-gapped deployment for sovereign AI.
  • AI-driven operations and orchestration exposing APIs that integrate with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, giving AI assistants access to operational data for smarter automation, faster troubleshooting, and proactive operations.
  • Cloud-native and container-native support for running both VNFs and cloud-native network functions (CNFs) on consistent horizontal infrastructure, enabling telcos to modernize at their own pace with flexible 2-year Long-Term Support (LTS) with every minor release of Kubernetes.
  • Multi-tenant isolation to meet business and compliance needs, keeping workloads from different tenants and domains securely separated.
  • Energy efficiency and sustainability are built into the platform through memory tiering and resource optimization. Enhanced NVMe memory tiering eliminates hardware redundant array of independent disks (RAID) dependency and reduces server total cost of ownership (TCO). Next-generation compression with global deduplication reduces storage footprint, lowering TCO compared to external traditional storage arrays.
  • Sovereign security and compliance, with in-jurisdiction operations, customer-controlled encryption keys, audit-grade evidence, automated policy enforcement aligned to standards such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the UK Telecommunications Security Act, quantum cryptography, and confidential computing. Zero-trust micro-segmentation is now optionally available with VMware vDefend.

What this means for existing Telco Cloud Platform customers

The future of the Telco Cloud brings network, IT, and AI workloads together on a single platform. By delivering these capabilities through VCF, telcos get a platform that scales from IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) and 4G virtualized workloads to cloud-native 5G services to AI-native workloads.  The work continues. The capabilities keep growing with every release, and the path to a simpler, more agile telco cloud is clearer than ever.

Next steps

  • Existing customers: No immediate action is needed. Your current Telco Cloud Platform subscription remains fully supported, along with all of its components, through the transition to VCF Telco. At renewal, your Broadcom representative works with you to align your go-forward requirements to VCF.
  • Existing VCF IT customers who would like to expand to VCF Telco: Your Broadcom account team can talk you through understanding the capabilities and options.
  • New and prospective customers: Your Broadcom account team can talk you through new capabilities and detailed migration paths.
  • Partners: Your Broadcom channel team can support you in understanding the capabilities that VCF Telco can bring to your telco customers.

For additional details, reach out to your Broadcom account team and sales representative.

item.title: VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.8: Advancing AI and Modern Workloads in Private Cloud
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) 3.8 cuts operational overhead, hardens the security baseline, and accelerates AI and modern application adoption for platform teams running Kubernetes on private cloud. The post VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.8: Advancing AI and Modern Workloads in Private Cloud appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) 3.8 cuts operational overhead, hardens the security baseline, and accelerates AI and modern application adoption for platform teams running Kubernetes on private cloud. Automated multi-version upgrades, granular workload placement, enterprise secrets integration, and Kubernetes-native CI/CD tooling give platform engineers the controls they need, while giving CIOs and CTOs the cost predictability and governance their organizations demand.

Enterprise IT leaders must balance three competing priorities: keeping operational overhead in check, maintaining a hardened security posture, and accelerate developer velocity and AI adoption. These three priorities are not isolated goals. They are interdependent pillars of a successful cloud-native strategy. Fast application delivery without embedded security creates enterprise risk, while heavy manual operations stall business innovation and increase the hidden cost in the total cost of ownership.

VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, a CNCF-certified Kubernetes runtime natively built in VMware Cloud Foundation, addresses these three imperatives in VKS 3.8. The release aligns rapid application delivery directly with automated security governance and zero-friction operations.

Reducing Operational Burden

In VKS 3.8, organizations can reduce operational overhead and reduce the risk of failure with automated chained upgrades. Granular resource management maximizes return on investment by preventing system workloads, such as the control plane workloads, from consuming high-cost, specialized hardware like the GPU resources. Flexibility in placement policies help optimize utilization of high-cost hardware assets and ensure business continuity for mission-critical applications. Together, these operational advances deliver a predictable, cost-effective infrastructure foundation that scales effortlessly alongside growing business demands.

Automated Chained Upgrades

VKS 3.8 orchestrates multi-version vSphere Kubernetes release upgrades automatically with built-in dependency checks and flag deprecation issues. This helps reduce the time spent in Day 2 operations and minimizes business disruption by reducing the maintenance window. 

Platform teams no longer face complex multi-hop upgrade scripting and manual dependency checks across incremental versions. Automated upgrades cordon and drain pods from worker nodes just once during the entire process rather than at each intermediate step, significantly accelerating execution and minimizing scheduling risks.

Granular Workload Placement Control

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 users can now leverage the new node placement enhancements in VKS 3.8 for granular infrastructure controls to address cost, capacity constraints, sovereignty, performance, and resiliency requirements. VKS now enables platform teams to programmatically pin a workload to a resource based on infrastructure policy. 

For example, an enterprise with an active-active stretched cluster can now explicitly assign distinct VKS node pools to a specific site. In the figure below, node pools within the cluster are pinned to specific sites for resiliency across control plane and worker nodes to manage stateful applications.

New control plane placement filtering allows platform teams to specify infrastructure policies to exclude high-cost compute clusters (such as dedicated GPU hardware) from control plane node scheduling. This approach prevents non-GPU control workloads from landing on expensive hosts while maintaining automated spreading across the remaining clusters.

Embedding Security and Compliance into Delivery Pipelines

By embedding automated security and governance directly into the platform lifecycle, VKS 3.8 helps organizations elevate their infrastructure security, protect intellectual property, and safeguard customer trust without sacrificing application velocity. Business leaders gain easier, faster audit readiness for stringent regulatory frameworks. Simultaneously, the enterprise significantly reduces its cyber risk surface — shielding critical infrastructure against unauthorized access, lateral threat movement, and credential leaks — helping ensure that rapid application delivery remains fully aligned with rigorous corporate governance.

Automated Admission Guardrails

VKS 3.8 builds on pre-configured policy sets to validate workloads at deployment using two add-ons delivered in prior releases: the VKS Policy Bundle add-on and the declarative Policy-as-Code using Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper add-on. These policy sets align with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the National Security Agency (NSA) Kubernetes hardening guidance, and the Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmark.

VKS 3.8 safeguards enterprise reputation and maintains audit readiness without slowing down application releases. Platform teams can automatically block non-compliant container configurations before they reach production.

Platform Hardening

VKS 3.8 programmatically disables SSH access across all Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes. This elevates the security baseline and eliminates ad-hoc operating system (OS)-level changes. The result is a hardened platform that reduces exposure to brute-force attacks and prevents lateral attacker movement across cluster infrastructure.

Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment

Using Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE), VKS 3.8 performs periodic integrity checks across critical system directories to detect unauthorized file changes. This gives infrastructure admins an automated mechanism to catch tampering without manual monitoring.

Centralized Credential Governance

VKS 3.8 synchronizes credentials dynamically from enterprise vaults including HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Secret Manager using the External Secrets Operator (ESO) add-on. This eliminates static credentials stored in code repositories and simplifies compliance audits for SOC2, PCI DSS, and HIPAA requirements. 

Platform teams can reduce exposure to data-at-rest vulnerabilities by removing plain-text secrets from Git repositories and YAML manifests while automating multi-cloud secret rotation.

Accelerating Developer Velocity and AI Adoption

VKS 3.8 brings fine-grained resource management to high-cost GPU hardware assets, enabling organizations to significantly boost infrastructure ROI while eliminating expensive idle capacity. Accelerated development workflows dramatically shorten product release cycles, allowing businesses to launch new capabilities faster while safeguarding the infrastructure through automated release integrity. 

Full-stack operational visibility protects ongoing revenue and the developer experience by enabling teams to resolve service disruptions rapidly. Together, these outcomes empower enterprises to achieve faster overall time-to-value for modern application initiatives and AI investments.

Native CI/CD Pipelines with Tekton

VKS 3.8 introduces Tekton for in-cluster continuous integration (CI) pipelines that automate code builds and testing. The pipelines sync natively with ArgoCD for continuous global fleet delivery, and they run inside the cluster using standard Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). 

Platform teams get a resource-efficient build environment without exposing clusters to external networks. The business impact shows up in shorter product release cycles and protect brand integrity through automated image signing and provenance.

Dynamic NVIDIA GPU Allocation1

Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) for NVIDIA GPUs will use the native Kubernetes DRA framework to dynamically assign and hot-attach physical or fractional GPUs on demand. Dynamic allocation will let teams share expensive GPU hardware across projects instead of leaving it idle. 

The business case is straightforward: maximize return on investment (ROI) on costly AI infrastructure by eliminating idle hardware and sharing GPUs across teams. For platform teams, it removes manual GPU provisioning friction while maintaining secure tenant isolation on shared GPU cards.

Full-Stack Observability with OpenTelemetry1

Open Telemetry (OTel) unifies traces, metrics, and logs across widely used applications like Java, Python, .NET, and Go into a single streaming framework. With consolidated visibility, OTel will help developers and platform teams reduce Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) and protect revenue and customer experience when issues arise. 

Instead of toggling between disparate monitoring tools, teams will get a unified view of application health across the full stack using observability tools like VCF Operations, Datadog, Splunk, or New Relic, among others.

VKS Quick Start1

VKS Quick Start accelerates time to value by deploying production-ready VKS Cluster, so developers can start building on Day 1. Platform teams can quickly enable the vSphere Supervisor with guided workflow and start running Kubernetes workloads. Teams can easily deploy essential add-ons and use the intuitive GUI to visualize clusters and resources for rapid workload testing.

Release Cadence and Support

By decoupling its release cadence from core platform upgrades, VKS 3.8 delivers Kubernetes 1.37 support within 60 days of CNCF upstream releases, backed by Broadcom’s 24-month extended support policy. When it is time for an upgrade the newly introduced automated chained upgrade helps enterprises capture the latest innovation in open source without skipping a beat. 

This predictability establishes a cohesive operational continuum for both business leaders and platform teams. Streamlined operations free platform teams from routine maintenance, allowing them to focus on onboarding new AI capabilities and accelerating business outcomes.

Plan for Success with VKS 3.8 

By significantly reducing the day-2 operational burden, accelerating time-to-value, and elevating the security baseline, VKS 3.8 helps enterprise organizations scale their private cloud infrastructure with confidence. This release continues to strengthen VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service as the proven enterprise Kubernetes platform for AI and modern workloads in private cloud environments. 

Resources

Blog: Deploy Modern Apps Faster, Scale Smarter, and Lower TCO with VKS in VCF 9.1

1 Will be delivered in a future release.

item.title: 第2回：仮想パッチを用いたセキュリティパッチ適用までの「猶予期間」の消滅
item.dc:creator: byungji kwon
item.description:
前回の「第1回：AI時代のプライベートクラウド多層防御、VMware Cloud Foundation®で実現する仮想基盤の堅牢化とリスク低減策」では、VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 環境におけるセキュリティの全体像と、ワークロードを保護するための多層防御アーキテクチャの重要性について解説しました。第1回公開後、多くのお客様から反響をいただき、特に内部トラフィックの可視化と制御に関する関心の高さを実感しております。 第2回となる今回は、企業のセキュリティ運用およびITインフラ管理者にとって恒常的な課題となっている「脆弱性公開からパッチ適用までの猶予期間（Vulnerability Window）」に焦点を当てます。この無防備となり得る期間の脅威をどのように無効化するかについて、VMware® vDefend™ (vDefend) の「分散IDS/IPS」と「VMware® Avi™ Load Balancer WAF (Web Application Firewall) 」を用いた「仮想パッチ」の技術を解説します。また、それらがもたらすダウンタイムの削減および運用コスト削減の具体的なメリットについて、技術的な観点から深掘りしてお届けします。   1. セキュリティパッチ適用の課題：「猶予期間」に潜むリスク 新しい脆弱性（CVE）が公開され、ベンダーからセキュリティパッチがリリースされた際、セキュリティのベストプラクティスとしては即座にパッチを適用することが推奨されます。しかし、エンタープライズの運用環境、特にミッションクリティカルなプライベートクラウド環境においては、以下のような理由から即時適用は非常に困難です。 ・アプリケーションへの影響検証：OSやミドルウェアへのパッチ適用が、稼働中の業務アプリケーションやAIモデルの推論プロセスに予期せぬ不具合（互換性の問題、パフォーマンス低下など）を引き起こさないか、事前環境でのテストが必要です。 ・ダウンタイムの調整：システムの再起動を伴うパッチ適用の場合、事業部門との調整を行い、影響を最小限に抑えるメンテナンスウィンドウ（計画停止枠）を確保する必要があります。 ・運用リソースの逼迫：緊急度の高い脆弱性が連続して公開された場合、IT部門の運用担当者への負荷が高まり、通常の運用業務に支障をきたす恐れがあります。 この「脆弱性が公開されてから、実際にシステムにパッチが適用されるまでの期間（猶予期間）」は、攻撃者にとってシステムへ侵入するための格好の標的となります。この期間をいかに安全に保護し、リスクを低減するかが、インフラ運用における重要な鍵となります。   2. 仮想パッチ（Virtual Patching）という解決策 この「猶予期間」の課題に対する有効な技術的アプローチが「仮想パッチ（Virtual Patching）」です。 仮想パッチとは、サーバーのOSやアプリケーションのコードに直接パッチを適用（修正）する代わりに、ネットワークの中間層で該当の脆弱性を突く攻撃トラフィックを検知し、遮断する手法です。これにより、システム本体には脆弱性が残った状態であっても、外部からのエクスプロイト（攻撃コード）が到達しないため、実質的にパッチが適用されたのと同じ防御効果を即座に得ることができます。 VCF環境においては、ネットワークの内部（East-West）と境界（North-South）のそれぞれで、最適な仮想パッチの仕組みを提供しています。   3. vDefend 分散IDS/IPSによるEast-Westトラフィックの保護 データセンター内部の通信（East-Westトラフィック）に対する仮想パッチとして機能するのが、「vDefend」の分散IDS/IPSです。 従来の境界型（アプライアンス型）IPSでは、一度データセンター内部に侵入した脅威が、仮想マシン間で横展開（ラテラルムーブメント）する動きを検知・遮断することが困難でした。すべての内部通信を境界アプライアンスにヘアピンさせるアーキテクチャは、ネットワーク帯域の浪費と遅延を引き起こすため現実的ではありません。 vDefendの分散IDS/IPSは、各ESXホストのハイパーバイザー（vNIC）レベルで直接動作します。これにより、ネットワークのトポロジ変更を一切伴わず、すべての仮想マシン間通信に対して死角なく仮想パッチ（シグネチャによる検知・防御）を適用することが可能です。   4. VMware Avi Load Balancer WAFによるアプリケーション層の保護 インフラストラクチャ層の保護に加えて、公開されているWebアプリケーション層（L7）の保護には「Avi Load Balancer WAF」が仮想パッチとして機能します。 Webアプリケーションの脆弱性（例：SQLインジェクション、クロスサイトスクリプティングなど）が発見された場合、アプリケーションのソースコードを修正してデプロイし直すには多大な時間とコストがかかります。Avi … Continued

item.content:encoded:
前回の「第1回：AI時代のプライベートクラウド多層防御、VMware Cloud Foundation®で実現する仮想基盤の堅牢化とリスク低減策」では、VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 環境におけるセキュリティの全体像と、ワークロードを保護するための多層防御アーキテクチャの重要性について解説しました。第1回公開後、多くのお客様から反響をいただき、特に内部トラフィックの可視化と制御に関する関心の高さを実感しております。 第2回となる今回は、企業のセキュリティ運用およびITインフラ管理者にとって恒常的な課題となっている「脆弱性公開からパッチ適用までの猶予期間（Vulnerability Window）」に焦点を当てます。この無防備となり得る期間の脅威をどのように無効化するかについて、VMware® vDefend (vDefend) の「分散IDS/IPS」と「VMware® Avi Load Balancer WAF (Web Application Firewall) 」を用いた「仮想パッチ」の技術を解説します。また、それらがもたらすダウンタイムの削減および運用コスト削減の具体的なメリットについて、技術的な観点から深掘りしてお届けします。   1. セキュリティパッチ適用の課題：「猶予期間」に潜むリスク 新しい脆弱性（CVE）が公開され、ベンダーからセキュリティパッチがリリースされた際、セキュリティのベストプラクティスとしては即座にパッチを適用することが推奨されます。しかし、エンタープライズの運用環境、特にミッションクリティカルなプライベートクラウド環境においては、以下のような理由から即時適用は非常に困難です。 ・アプリケーションへの影響検証：OSやミドルウェアへのパッチ適用が、稼働中の業務アプリケーションやAIモデルの推論プロセスに予期せぬ不具合（互換性の問題、パフォーマンス低下など）を引き起こさないか、事前環境でのテストが必要です。 ・ダウンタイムの調整：システムの再起動を伴うパッチ適用の場合、事業部門との調整を行い、影響を最小限に抑えるメンテナンスウィンドウ（計画停止枠）を確保する必要があります。 ・運用リソースの逼迫：緊急度の高い脆弱性が連続して公開された場合、IT部門の運用担当者への負荷が高まり、通常の運用業務に支障をきたす恐れがあります。 この「脆弱性が公開されてから、実際にシステムにパッチが適用されるまでの期間（猶予期間）」は、攻撃者にとってシステムへ侵入するための格好の標的となります。この期間をいかに安全に保護し、リスクを低減するかが、インフラ運用における重要な鍵となります。   2. 仮想パッチ（Virtual Patching）という解決策 この「猶予期間」の課題に対する有効な技術的アプローチが「仮想パッチ（Virtual Patching）」です。 仮想パッチとは、サーバーのOSやアプリケーションのコードに直接パッチを適用（修正）する代わりに、ネットワークの中間層で該当の脆弱性を突く攻撃トラフィックを検知し、遮断する手法です。これにより、システム本体には脆弱性が残った状態であっても、外部からのエクスプロイト（攻撃コード）が到達しないため、実質的にパッチが適用されたのと同じ防御効果を即座に得ることができます。 VCF環境においては、ネットワークの内部（East-West）と境界（North-South）のそれぞれで、最適な仮想パッチの仕組みを提供しています。   3. vDefend 分散IDS/IPSによるEast-Westトラフィックの保護 データセンター内部の通信（East-Westトラフィック）に対する仮想パッチとして機能するのが、「vDefend」の分散IDS/IPSです。 従来の境界型（アプライアンス型）IPSでは、一度データセンター内部に侵入した脅威が、仮想マシン間で横展開（ラテラルムーブメント）する動きを検知・遮断することが困難でした。すべての内部通信を境界アプライアンスにヘアピンさせるアーキテクチャは、ネットワーク帯域の浪費と遅延を引き起こすため現実的ではありません。 vDefendの分散IDS/IPSは、各ESXホストのハイパーバイザー（vNIC）レベルで直接動作します。これにより、ネットワークのトポロジ変更を一切伴わず、すべての仮想マシン間通信に対して死角なく仮想パッチ（シグネチャによる検知・防御）を適用することが可能です。   4. VMware Avi Load Balancer WAFによるアプリケーション層の保護 インフラストラクチャ層の保護に加えて、公開されているWebアプリケーション層（L7）の保護には「Avi Load Balancer WAF」が仮想パッチとして機能します。 Webアプリケーションの脆弱性（例：SQLインジェクション、クロスサイトスクリプティングなど）が発見された場合、アプリケーションのソースコードを修正してデプロイし直すには多大な時間とコストがかかります。Avi … Continued

item.title: Good Fences, Good Neighbors: Isolating Infrastructure Management
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
(Day 20 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: isolating the management network) Robert Frost’s poem “Mending Wall” gave us the line “good fences make good neighbors,” though the poem itself is actually skeptical of the idea. Infrastructure security needs no such skepticism. The management network, where vCenter, ESX, NSX, and the rest … Continued

The post Good Fences, Good Neighbors: Isolating Infrastructure Management appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
(Day 20 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: isolating the management network)

Robert Frost’s poem “Mending Wall” gave us the line “good fences make good neighbors,” though the poem itself is actually skeptical of the idea. Infrastructure security needs no such skepticism. The management network, where vCenter, ESX, NSX, and the rest of the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) management components live, holds the keys to everything running on the platform, and it deserves a good fence.

Why Attackers Go After the Management Network

An attacker who reaches the management network can do in minutes what would otherwise take weeks: encrypt every VM at once, copy domain controllers, delete backups, and stay out of sight of the security tools running inside the guests. Threat intelligence reports say it outright: ransomware operators actively target backup infrastructure, identity services, and virtualization management planes, and virtualization and management platforms need to be treated as Tier 0 assets (Google’s M-Trends 2026 report).

The paths in tend to look alike:

  • Management interfaces exposed where they shouldn’t be. One ransomware campaign compromised more than 3,800 internet-exposed, unpatched hypervisor hosts around the world (CISA and FBI). Without further defense-in-depth, a vulnerability is easily exploited, and stolen credentials are easily used.
  • Flat networks. Threat researchers describe attackers moving from a help desk call to Active Directory, to vCenter, to ESX, to ransomware “in mere hours” (Google Threat Intelligence Group report). Each step was easier because the next system was reachable from the last one.
  • Unrestricted outbound access. Attackers have planted backdoors on management appliances that call out to the internet for instructions, and investigators recommend that appliances not have unrestricted access to the internet (Google Cloud blog).

Good isolation won’t stop every attack, but it takes away the shortcuts and makes attackers much more likely to get caught.

What Belongs on the Management Network

In VCF, the management network holds vCenter, NSX Manager, SDDC Manager, VCF Operations and its related components, fleet management, VCF Identity Broker, and VCF Automation (management appliances), along with the ESX management interfaces and the VCF management services. Add the things those components depend on, like DNS, NTP, key servers, backup targets, and log collectors. Server hardware management controllers belong on the list, too, which we talk about below.

VCF’s design guidance separates these further. ESX management traffic gets its own VLAN, apart from the other management components, and each workload domain gets its own ESX management VLAN (ESX design). Each host’s management VMkernel interface belongs on that dedicated segment, with other VMkernel interfaces carrying only their own traffic. That way, “an intruder on a non-management segment cannot directly initiate a management session against the host” (VCF Security Configuration Guide).

Build the Fence

Separate networks are a start, but VLANs by themselves don’t provide isolation. Broadcom’s ransomware design guidance puts it well: several VLANs may still allow one administrator, jump host, or broad firewall rule to reach everything, and “that changes the diagram more than the risk” (ransomware design). The fence is the firewall policy between those networks.

The VCF Security Configuration Guide says management interfaces should be reachable “only from the networks administrators use, not from general user or workload networks and not from the internet.” Administrators should connect from an authorized network or through a jump host. Build that with a perimeter firewall around the management network, and then tighten the gates on each component:

  • Restrict the ESX firewall. By default, the firewall rule for each ESX service allows access from any IP address. Change each service to allow only your management networks (docs).
  • Use lockdown mode. Normal lockdown mode routes host management through vCenter. It doesn’t turn off SSH or the ESX Shell, so keep those services stopped, and reserve the Exception Users list for service accounts (lockdown behavior). Be careful with strict lockdown mode: if vCenter is lost and no other path was prepared, recovering a host may mean reinstalling it (KB 336894).
  • Use the appliance firewalls carefully. The vCenter appliance firewall filters inbound traffic by source address, for all ports at once (tech docs), so add a rule for your administrative networks first, or you can lock yourself out. It doesn’t filter outbound traffic, which is a job for the perimeter firewall.
  • Turn on VCF Operations firewall hardening, which limits traffic between cluster nodes and is off by default.
  • Remove what you don’t need. Power off or remove the VCF Installer after bring-up, unless it became SDDC Manager, because it holds bring-up credentials and would otherwise just be another thing to patch and maintain.

Don’t Forget the Basement Door

Every server has a hardware management controller, often called a BMC, that provides remote console, power control, and firmware updates, and it keeps working even when the server is powered off. NSA and CISA call the firmware in these controllers “highly privileged,” warn that attackers could use them to disable security features like the TPM, and recommend isolating BMC network connections (NSA and CISA). Attackers are paying attention, too; CISA has added an authentication bypass in a widely used BMC firmware to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities (CISA).

Our post on hardware security covers these controllers in more depth. For the management network, the VCF Security Configuration Guide recommends treating them as Tier 0:

  • Put them on a dedicated management interface, or at least an isolated VLAN, reachable only from authorized administrative addresses.
  • Turn off services you don’t use, like IPMI over LAN, and require TLS 1.2 or later, and TLS 1.3 where the controller supports it.
  • Don’t authenticate BMC users against an Active Directory that runs on the same hosts the BMCs can power off. It’s a dependency loop, at best, and connections to identity providers are also attack paths.
  • Lock the configuration after provisioning, forward the logs, and sync the time.

Control the Way In and the Way Out

The way in. Administrators should reach the management network from a small number of controlled places. Microsoft’s guidance on privileged access workstations, dedicated devices for administration that don’t do email or web browsing, applies to infrastructure administrators as much as anyone (Microsoft). If you use jump hosts, remember that a jump host many sensitive sessions pass through is a target in its own right. Microsoft’s tier model treats a jump server used to reach domain controllers as a Tier 0 asset (tier model). NSA’s guidance on out-of-band management goes further, calling physically separate management infrastructure the most secure design (NSA).

The way out. Management components need very little from the internet, so give them very little. VCF needs to reach a short list of Broadcom URLs on port 443 (public URLs). Send that traffic through a proxy, and block the rest. A few options make it easier:

  • Use a proxy. VCF Operations, SDDC Manager, and vCenter all support proxies, and TLS-inspecting proxies work with some extra configuration, like importing the proxy’s CA certificate.
  • Use an offline depot. The VCF Download Tool fills an offline depot from a system with internet access, and one depot can serve multiple VCF instances (tech docs).
  • Turn off defaults that call out. For example, vCenter downloads the vSAN hardware compatibility list directly from the internet unless you turn that off or send it through a proxy.

Broadcom’s guidance on the BRICKSTORM backdoor recommends restricting outbound internet access from vCenter and ESX (KB 427833). An appliance that can’t call out is much less useful to an attacker who has compromised it.

Good Fences Make Good Management Networks

Isolation isn’t glamorous, and it rarely shows up in a product demo. It’s also one of the most effective things you can do for infrastructure management. Know what lives on the management network, put a real firewall around it, tighten the gates on each component, give the hardware controllers their own fence, and control the ways in and out.

item.title: Workloads Keeping Secrets: Confidential Computing
item.dc:creator: bob plankers
item.description:
(Day 19 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: confidential computing) Data has three states. It’s at rest when it’s stored, in transit when it’s moving across a network, and in use when it’s being processed. Other posts in this series cover the first two, with storage encryption and network encryption. The third … Continued

The post Workloads Keeping Secrets: Confidential Computing appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
(Day 19 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: confidential computing)

Data has three states. It’s at rest when it’s stored, in transit when it’s moving across a network, and in use when it’s being processed. Other posts in this series cover the first two, with storage encryption and network encryption. The third has always been the hard one, because to do anything with data, the processor has to see it, and anything that controls the processor, like an operating system or a hypervisor, can see it, too.

Confidential computing changes that. It uses features built into modern AMD and Intel processors to keep a virtual machine’s memory encrypted and isolated from everything outside the VM, including the hypervisor and the people who run it, and VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) supports confidential VMs on both.

What Confidential Computing Protects Against

The Confidential Computing Consortium defines confidential computing as “the protection of data in use by performing computation in a hardware-based, attested Trusted Execution Environment” (CCC). In practice, the processor manages a separate key for each confidential VM and encrypts the VM’s memory with it. The hypervisor doesn’t hold those keys, so even someone with administrative access to an ESX host can’t use the hypervisor to read a confidential VM’s memory in cleartext (confidential computing in VCF).

That matters because whoever controls a hypervisor can normally see everything inside the VMs it runs. A memory snapshot, like the ones in our post on snapshots, captures the passwords, keys, and data of a running VM. That’s useful to incident responders, and just as useful to an attacker who has gained administrative access. Attackers can also arrive from below: one exploited chain of vulnerabilities let someone with administrative access inside a guest escape to the host, where the memory of every other VM would normally be within reach.

Confidential computing largely takes memory off the table for those attackers. It’s a good fit for workloads like key management systems, secure databases, regulated workloads, and private AI, where the data in memory is the most valuable thing on the system.

How Confidential VMs Work

VCF supports one processor technology from each vendor:

  • AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging), on AMD EPYC processors from the Milan generation onward. It encrypts VM memory and adds integrity protection that keeps the hypervisor from replaying or remapping a VM’s memory (AMD).
  • Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions), on 5th Gen Intel Xeon processors and later. It runs each confidential VM in a hardware-isolated trust domain, protecting the confidentiality and integrity of its memory and CPU state (Intel).

Hosts that run confidential VMs can use Quick Boot, too. Setup has three parts: turn on the processor features in each server’s firmware, use virtual hardware version 22 or later, and choose the confidential VM mode under VM Options > Confidential Compute while the VM is powered off (SEV-SNP, TDX). Confidential VMs run Linux guests with recent kernels, and Broadcom lists the validated guest operating systems in KB 401005.

VCF Operations shows which hosts support confidential VMs, whether the feature is turned on, and which VMs are confidential. The VCF Security and Compliance Guidelines repository has a detailed set of questions and answers about confidential computing in VCF, and the VMware Cloud Foundation YouTube channel has a video on it, too:

Attestation: Proving It’s Real

Encrypting memory is only half of confidential computing. The other half is attestation, which lets a workload, or the people who own it, verify that it’s running in a genuine, correctly configured trusted execution environment before trusting it with secrets. NIST describes attestation as verifiable cryptographic evidence that lets a relying party send secrets directly into the protected environment (NIST IR 8320).

The processor signs a report describing the confidential VM, and a verifier checks that report against the processor vendor’s certificates (details):

  • AMD SEV-SNP guests generate an attestation report from inside the guest and verify it against AMD’s published certificates using open source tools. SEV-SNP can also check a VM’s expected measurements before it’s allowed to start.
  • Intel TDX guests generate a signed quote through the Linux kernel, using an attestation component installed on each host, and the quote is verified using Intel’s services.

The evidence goes to whatever verifier you choose, often a key management or secrets system that releases keys only to VMs that pass. Design that flow up front, because attestation only helps when something acts on the result.

What Confidential VMs Don’t Protect Against

Confidential computing is a strong control with a specific scope. It doesn’t protect against:

  • Problems inside the guest. A vulnerable application, a weak password, or malware running in the VM sees the same cleartext memory the workload does. The guest still needs patching and hardening, and it should treat anything coming from the host as untrusted (Linux kernel threat model).
  • Data on disk. Confidential computing covers data in use. Attackers who reach vCenter have cloned sensitive VMs, like domain controllers, and read their disks offline (report), and memory encryption doesn’t stop that. Encrypt a confidential VM’s disks from inside the guest, ideally with keys that are released only after a successful attestation.
  • Denial of service. The hypervisor still decides when a VM runs and what resources it gets, so someone who controls a host can still stop a confidential VM.
  • Sophisticated physical attacks. The consortium’s definition puts these out of scope, and researchers have shown attacks that use tampered memory modules to undermine these protections, which processor makers have addressed with firmware updates (example). Keep server firmware current, and keep physical security in place.

Operational Trade-Offs to Plan For

Confidential VMs give up some of the conveniences that make virtualization pleasant, because many of those conveniences depend on the hypervisor being able to see or copy a VM’s memory. Confidential VMs don’t support:

  • vMotion, so plan maintenance around powering VMs off, or around failover at the application level.
  • Memory snapshots, memory tiering, or suspend and resume.
  • Fault Tolerance, or hot-adding CPU and memory.
  • A virtual TPM or Secure Boot inside the guest, so the advice in our post on VM security features doesn’t fully carry over.
  • VMware Tools inside Intel TDX guests.

A few more things to plan for:

  • Linux guests only. The validated guest list is specific, but industry support is growing (KB 401005).
  • Memory is fully reserved. All of a confidential VM’s memory is reserved on the host, and hosts using Intel TDX also set aside memory for the processor’s security features, so capacity planning changes.
  • Attestation needs a path. Intel TDX attestation relies on Intel’s remote provisioning and verification services, so isolated environments need a plan for reaching them.
  • Firmware settings matter. The processor features have to be turned on in each server’s firmware, consistently across the cluster, and the VCF Security Configuration Guide includes controls for it.

Where Confidential Computing Fits

Not every VM needs confidential computing. Most workloads are well served by the features in our post on VM security, along with storage encryption and good access control. Confidential computing earns its trade-offs for workloads where the data in memory is the crown jewels, like key management systems, secrets vaults, sensitive databases, regulated workloads, and private AI models and the data they process.

Start small. Pick one workload, check that your servers and guest operating systems are on the supported lists, work out how attestation will control the release of secrets, and plan around the operational trade-offs. Use VCF Operations to keep track of which hosts are ready and which VMs are confidential.

Every workload trusts the infrastructure it runs on. With confidential computing, it can trust a little less.

item.title: Why VMware Memory Tiering is Not Just Swapping to NVMe
item.dc:creator: vmwareblogs
item.description:
Why VMware Memory Tiering is not just swapping to NVMe Memory is one of the most expensive resources in the data center, and workloads keep asking for more of it. We pack more VMs onto each host to get the most out of the hardware investment, but DRAM has a ceiling, both physical and financial. … Continued

The post Why VMware Memory Tiering is Not Just Swapping to NVMe appeared first on VMware Blogs.
item.content:encoded:
Why VMware Memory Tiering is not just swapping to NVMe

Memory is one of the most expensive resources in the data center, and workloads keep asking for more of it. We pack more VMs onto each host to get the most out of the hardware investment, but DRAM has a ceiling, both physical and financial. When memory runs short, the question comes up. Is Memory Tiering just swapping to NVMe?

We get this question a lot. Swapping is the boat is sinking. Memory Tiering is let’s steer away from that iceberg so we don’t sink. One is a desperate scramble after the fact. The other is a deliberate course correction before you hit trouble.

What swapping actually does

Swapping has been around for a long time. When a host runs out of memory and needs to reclaim some fast, the hypervisor picks pages and writes them out to disk to make room. It is a last resort, the equivalent of bailing water over the side because the hull has already been breached. The goal is correctness, keeping the system running when memory is exhausted.

The catch is that swapping does not care which pages it moves. A hot page that your application needs in the next millisecond can get swapped out right alongside a cold page that nobody has touched since boot. When that hot page is needed again, it has to be read back from disk, and performance takes a hit. You are bailing blindly, throwing important cargo overboard along with the ballast.

How Memory Tiering works differently

Broadcom, through its portfolio of VMware products, introduced Memory Tiering in VMware Cloud Foundation to extend host memory using NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) devices alongside traditional DRAM (dynamic random access memory). The result is a single logical memory space that VMs consume without knowing or caring which tier their pages live on, transparent to your applications.

Memory Tiering does not wait for a crisis. It runs continuously in the background, scanning VM memory pages in batches and classifying them as hot or cold using two signals. Recency tells us how recently a page was accessed. Frequency tells us how often it gets accessed. Hot pages stay in Tier 0, which is DRAM. Cold pages migrate to Tier 1, which is NVMe.

This is the core difference. Swap uses a simplistic random selection of pages. Memory Tiering uses sophisticated page aging techniques that classify pages by recency and frequency before deciding where they belong. Only cold pages move to NVMe, and hot pages stay in DRAM, with a small CPU footprint of roughly an eighth of a core on smaller hosts. Swap can touch any memory pages, including kernel memory under extreme conditions, but Memory Tiering only applies to VM memory pages, so the hypervisor itself always runs on fast DRAM.

Memory Tiering starts considering page movement when a threshold is reached. That threshold is not a fixed number. It is computed based on several conditions, including the current memory state, which in turn depends on minFree. minFree is not the amount of free memory on the host at a given moment. It is a computed target the VMkernel maintains as a safety buffer, derived from a sliding scale based on host memory size. The configuration of your hosts, the workloads running on them, and other variables all feed into where that line gets drawn. You might wonder why it waits for a threshold at all if it is supposed to be proactive. We want to keep most pages in DRAM as long as we can, because DRAM is where performance lives. The threshold is not a crisis point. It is spotting the iceberg on the horizon and adjusting course early, while there is still plenty of open water. The system is not fighting for resources. It is making a planned decision about page placement while there is still headroom.

From that point on, the tiering algorithm monitors page activity across both tiers and moves pages between DRAM and NVMe as workloads change. It moves cold pages to NVMe. Not hot pages, the way swap does. The pages your applications actually need stay right where they belong, in fast DRAM.

A practical example

Say you have a host with 1 TB of DRAM and 1 TB of NVMe configured for Memory Tiering. One of the VMs on it is a database server with a 512 GB memory allocation. The database has an active working set of about 200 GB that it accesses constantly. The remaining 312 GB holds cached data and rarely accessed buffers.

Without Memory Tiering, all 512 GB sits in DRAM, and you are paying for expensive memory that is mostly idle. With Memory Tiering, the hypervisor identifies the 200 GB working set as hot and keeps it in DRAM. The 312 GB of cold cache pages gradually migrates to NVMe. Your database still performs well because the pages it actually needs are in fast DRAM.

Now imagine the same scenario with swapping instead. The host hits memory pressure, and the hypervisor starts moving random pages to disk. Some might be part of the active working set, so the database stalls waiting for disk reads. You waited until the hull was taking on water, and now you are bailing out the good cargo along with the bad.

What this means in practice

This is where looking into your workload patterns pays off. Memory Tiering performs well when your active memory fits within your DRAM capacity. The default configuration uses a 1-to-1 DRAM-to-NVMe ratio, up to a maximum of 4 TB of NVMe tiering capacity. If your workloads have a lot of cold memory, which many do, you can extend your effective memory capacity significantly.

By placing cold pages on NVMe instead of buying more DRAM, you lower your total cost of ownership (TCO) per VM without sacrificing performance for the workloads that matter. You also get more consolidation, which means fewer hosts to power, cool, and manage. That translates to headroom for growth without a proportional jump in hardware spend.

The bottom line

If you have been thinking of Memory Tiering as just fancy swapping, give it a closer look. Pair it with the right NVMe drives and a sensible sizing strategy, and you get memory capacity and performance without choosing between them. Check out the Memory Tiering documentation for VMware Cloud Foundation to see how to configure it on your hosts, and start small with a 1-to-1 ratio to see the difference for yourself. The iceberg is a lot easier to avoid when you can see it coming.

item.content:encoded:
(Day 18 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: VM security features)

Most of this series so far has focused on the infrastructure itself: hardware, hosts, management, and the networks in between. The virtual machines running on that infrastructure have security features of their own, though. Many of them sit unused simply because a VM was built from an old template, migrated from an older platform, or created in a hurry.

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) gives every virtual machine the same kinds of protections that modern physical servers have: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, a TPM, virtualization-based security, and encryption. Let’s go through them and take a look.

Build VM Security on UEFI and Secure Boot

Everything else in this post builds on UEFI firmware. Legacy BIOS firmware can’t do Secure Boot, can’t host a virtual TPM, and can’t run virtualization-based security, so the first step is making sure VMs use EFI firmware.

Secure Boot checks the signatures on the boot loader, kernel, and drivers before they load, which helps keep out malware that tries to hide underneath the operating system. It needs EFI firmware, virtual hardware version 13 or later, and a guest operating system that supports it. The VM has to be powered off to turn it on. The VCF Security Configuration Guide treats it as a top VM security priority.

A few things to know:

  • Converting from BIOS to UEFI takes work. Broadcom’s guidance for VMs that use virtualization-based security is to reinstall the guest (VBS best practices). Microsoft’s MBR2GPT tool can convert Windows 10 and 11 system disks in place (Microsoft), but test it, and take a snapshot first.
  • Secure Boot depends on updates. Secure Boot relies on lists of trusted and revoked signatures. The BlackLotus bootkit got around Secure Boot by loading older, vulnerable boot managers that were still validly signed, and the NSA’s guidance for mitigating it notes that virtual machines are affected, too (NSA). Keeping guests patched keeps those lists current.
  • Microsoft’s 2011 Secure Boot certificates are being replaced. Several Microsoft certificates that Secure Boot relies on expire in 2026. VMs keep booting, but VMs created on older versions of ESX, and the templates they came from, may not accept future Secure Boot updates until their certificates are refreshed. VCF raises a vCenter alarm for VMs that need the update and can update many of them automatically, and Broadcom’s guidance walks through the rest (KB 423893). You need to be running VCF 9.1.1 or a future vSphere 8.0 update, as well as VMware Tools 13.1.5 or newer, for these alarms and helpers to be present.

Give Windows a Virtual TPM

A virtual TPM (vTPM) is a software TPM 2.0 device that gives a VM the same kind of protected key storage that a physical TPM gives a physical server. Windows 11 requires a TPM 2.0 (Microsoft), and Windows uses it for BitLocker, Windows Hello, measured boot, and more.

A vTPM needs EFI firmware, virtual hardware version 14 or later, and a key provider, because its secrets are stored in the VM’s NVRAM file, which VM encryption protects. The Native Key Provider is enough, and with a vTPM, the standard resilience features, like vMotion, HA, and DRS, continue to work (vTPM overview). Our post on key provider design covers the keys.

Three details trip people up:

  • A vTPM doesn’t encrypt the virtual disks. Adding one encrypts the VM’s home files, like NVRAM and swap, and vCenter shows the VM as encrypted. The disks stay as they were, though, unless you also apply VM encryption, run atop an encrypted vSAN datastore, or use BitLocker inside the guest (vTPM overview). All of these things are compatible with vTPM-enabled VMs, too.
  • Clones copy the vTPM by default. Cloning a VM with a vTPM offers the choice of duplicating its TPM identity and secrets (the default, to match historical behavior) or replacing the vTPM with a blank copy. Replacing it destroys anything sealed to the old one, such as BitLocker keys, so suspend BitLocker first (KB 452119). Templates deserve special attention here, where you probably want to replace the vTPM.
  • Encrypted VMs can’t be exported as OVF or OVA files. That includes VMs with a vTPM, so keep their templates in a content library as VM templates. You can also use an OVF template with a vTPM placeholder, which gives each VM deployed from it a new vTPM with its own secrets (tech docs).

Turn On Virtualization-Based Security

Virtualization-based security (VBS) is a Windows feature that uses the hypervisor built into Windows to wall off a region of memory from the rest of the operating system. Windows uses it for Credential Guard, which protects credentials like NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets from theft (Microsoft), and for memory integrity, also called HVCI, which makes it much harder to load malicious code into the kernel (Microsoft). Newer versions of Windows turn Credential Guard on by default when the hardware supports it, so turning on VBS in the VM may be most of the work.

In VCF, VBS is a checkbox in the VM’s settings, and you then turn on the features you want inside Windows (VBS best practices). You don’t need to install the Hyper-V role in the guest, because Windows handles that itself. It needs EFI firmware and Secure Boot, along with virtual hardware version 14 or later on Intel hosts, or 19 or later on AMD hosts. Plan for the trade-offs:

  • Some features don’t mix with VBS. Fault Tolerance, PCI passthrough (which also impacts how GPUs might be consumed), and hot-adding CPU or memory aren’t supported on VBS-enabled VMs.
  • Performance depends on the CPU. Memory integrity runs best on newer processors with hardware support for it, where the overhead tends not to be noticeable and is worth the trade-off even when it is, but test with your own workloads.
  • Drivers matter. Memory integrity can block incompatible drivers, so test before rolling it out widely.

VBS walls are built by the guest’s own hypervisor, which runs on top of ESX, so VBS doesn’t protect a guest from someone who controls the host; Microsoft says as much about memory integrity. Protecting a VM’s memory from the host is a job for confidential computing.

Choose Where to Encrypt

Physical servers usually get disk encryption from the operating system, like BitLocker on Windows or LUKS on Linux, with keys protected by the server’s TPM. VMs with a vTPM can work the same way. In VCF, though, encrypting inside every guest usually isn’t necessary. vSAN data-at-rest encryption encrypts every VM’s disks without any changes to the guests and keeps vSAN’s compression and deduplication savings. Our post on storage encryption covers this, along with VM encryption for other storage.

vSAN encryption protects the data on the drives, but it’s transparent to anything that reads through the hypervisor, so someone who can clone a VM or download its files through vCenter gets readable data. Encrypting inside the guest adds a layer against that for the VMs that hold the keys to everything else, like domain controllers, certificate authorities, and secrets vaults. For those:

  • Give them a vTPM. BitLocker protects its keys with a TPM, and LUKS can, too, so give guests that encrypt their disks a vTPM, just as you’d give a physical server a TPM.
  • Add a BitLocker pre-boot PIN for the most critical VMs. Someone with enough privileges in vCenter can clone a VM and start the copy, and because the clone gets a copy of the vTPM, BitLocker unlocks it, too, unless it needs a PIN at startup. The PIN has to be entered after every restart, so save it for systems like domain controllers, where that operational trade-off is worth it.
  • Control who can decrypt, and who can copy. Encryption only helps if the people who shouldn’t see the data also don’t hold the cryptographic privileges. So give most administrators the built-in No Cryptography Administrator role and keep cryptographic privileges with a small group (docs). Privileges that copy a VM, like cloning, exporting, and downloading files from a datastore, deserve the same care.
  • Weigh the costs. Data encrypted inside the guest doesn’t compress or deduplicate, on vSAN or in your backup system. Every guest also needs its own recovery keys, stored somewhere you can reach when that VM is down, and for domain controllers, that shouldn’t be only the Active Directory they serve. The encryption also uses some guest CPU, so double-encrypting data on disk needs to be tested and thought through.

VM Security Settings: What’s Already Done and What to Change

Older hardening guides were full of VM settings to change. Many of those are now the defaults, and the VCF Security Configuration Guide lists them so you can audit them instead of setting them again. Copy, paste, and drag-and-drop between the console and the guest are off, as are disk shrinking, disk wiping, and connecting or disconnecting devices from inside the guest, and guests can’t read details about the host they run on. If you find any of them turned back on, find out why.

A handful of VM security settings still need changing:

  • Limit console connections. Set RemoteDisplay.maxConnections to 1, so nobody can watch an administrator’s session through a second console connection. Keep in mind, though, that if your session is disconnected via network instability you might have to wait until it times out to reconnect.
  • Lock the console on disconnect. For Windows guests, set tools.guest.desktop.autolock to TRUE, so closing the console doesn’t leave a logged-in session for the next person.
  • Boot only from disk. Set bios.bootDeviceClasses to allow:hd, and allow the CD drive only while you’re installing an operating system.
  • Remove hardware you don’t use. Every virtual device is code that a guest can talk to. When a critical vulnerability turned up in virtual USB controllers, the workaround was removing USB controllers from VMs (VMSA-2024-0006). Test first, because some devices are less optional than they look; removing the USB controller can affect console input in some guests, for example.
  • Keep virtual hardware current. The guide recommends hardware version 17 or later. Newer virtual hardware versions have performance and security improvements, as well as better compatibility with new physical hardware.
  • Set encrypted vMotion to Required for sensitive VMs. The default, Opportunistic, already encrypts migrations whenever both hosts support it, which current hosts do, and Required makes sure a migration is never sent in the clear (docs). Adding a vTPM or VM encryption switches a VM to Required automatically. Set encrypted Fault Tolerance to Required, too, for VMs that use it.

Lock Down VMware Tools

VMware Tools matters for VM security, too, and it has security settings of its own in each guest’s tools.conf file. The VCF Security Configuration Guide covers them, and you can change each one with the VMwareToolboxCmd utility that comes with Tools, as in “VMwareToolboxCmd config set guestoperations disabled true”, or by editing tools.conf. These are the ones to change:

  • Turn off guest operations where you don’t need them. Guest operations let vCenter run commands, move files, and list processes inside a guest. This makes them handy for automation and just as handy for an attacker who gets into vCenter. Many backup, disaster recovery, and automation tools depend on them, so check first, and leave them on in templates, because guest customization needs them.
  • Prevent re-customization of deployed VMs. Guest customization can run scripts as root or Administrator, so someone with access to vCenter could use it on a deployed VM to reset the Administrator password or add an account of their own. Set deployPkg enable-customization to false once a VM is deployed, unless something like a disaster recovery plan uses customization to change its IP address. Leave it on in templates, or the VMs you deploy from them won’t customize.
  • Turn off inventory features you don’t use. Application, service, and container discovery (appinfo, servicediscovery, and containerinfo) report what’s running in a guest to vCenter, where tools like VCF Operations use the data for application monitoring and dependency mapping. Leave them on where you use that data, and turn them off everywhere else.
  • Keep upgrades from changing features. Set autoupgrade allow-add-feature and allow-remove-feature to false, so automatic upgrades patch the Tools features you have without adding or removing any. Set gueststoreupgrade policy to off unless you deliver Tools upgrades through GuestStore.
  • Send Tools logs to the guest’s system log. Set the Tools logging handlers to syslog, which routes Tools activity to syslog on Linux and the event log on Windows, so whatever already ships the guest’s logs picks it up, too.
  • Keep VMware Tools current. It’s software like any other, and our post on patching applies to it, too. Linux distributions ship open-vm-tools, which updates with the rest of the guest’s packages, and for Windows, leave automatic Tools upgrades on unless you update Tools another way.

A few Tools settings are already where the guide wants them, like GlobalConf, which can push tools.conf changes to guests from a central source and is off by default, so audit those. The guide’s PowerCLI scripts audit and remediate the VM settings in the previous section and check whether Tools is current (tools). But tools.conf lives inside each guest, so set these with the configuration management you already use for the guest operating system.

Make VM Security Features the Default

The easiest VM security is the kind nobody has to remember. Build these features into your templates and content libraries: EFI firmware, Secure Boot, a current hardware version, a vTPM for Windows, VBS where the workload supports it, unneeded devices removed, and the recommended Tools settings in place. Leave guest operations and customization on, though, because templates need them. New VMs then start out with these protections in place, and the work shifts to the VMs that already exist.

For those, start your VM security work with the VMs that matter most, like domain controllers, certificate authorities, secrets vaults, and anything else an attacker would love to copy, and work outward from there. Every VM you bring up to date is one less easy target.
